lines: A real buffer handle crosses the boundary through an allocate function and a free function.
After that handle is correctly freed once, what happens when the identical handle is freed a second time?
answer: The handle is no longer live, so there is nothing left to free.

lines: Run it for real: every correct pair is accepted exactly once, a second free on the same handle is genuinely turned away rather than carried out, and no handle is ever left outstanding afterward.
A status function writes its real result through an out pointer instead, since there is no proper result type crossing this particular boundary.
When the real call genuinely fails, what happens to that out pointer?
answer: Only the status code itself reports that anything went wrong.

lines: Run it for real: a genuine success writes the real value through the out pointer, and a genuine failure returns its own status code while leaving that out pointer genuinely untouched.
steps.takeaway: A status code is only half the error protocol; where the real answer actually gets written matters just as much.

lines: A real function on the other side of the boundary genuinely panics when it is told to.
When a real caller catches that panic, does the caller genuinely keep running afterward?
answer: This exact calling convention defines what crossing with an unwind is allowed to mean.

lines: Run it for real: the real panic crossing that boundary is genuinely caught, and the caller genuinely keeps running right afterward, exactly as that convention defines.
steps.takeaway: That calling convention is not a suggestion; it genuinely defines what crossing with an unwind means.

lines: Two real, independent sources name this identical protocol directly, in their own words.

A foreign library handing off a resource's ownership needs a real destructor to guarantee it actually gets released, and a boundary expecting a panic to cross it has to say so explicitly in its own calling convention.
steps.takeaway: A calling convention's string names only the visible fraction of a protocol both sides keep by hand.

lines: So here's what this topic's own three small boundaries are really standing in for: matching a foreign struct's own layout gets you through the door, but it tells you nothing about who is actually on the hook for freeing what you're handed.
It tells you nothing about where a real failure's answer actually lands, and it tells you nothing about what happens the instant something on the other side of that door genuinely goes wrong.

Those three questions are a real, unenforced agreement two sides have to keep by hand, every single time, which is exactly why this chapter calls a boundary like this a protocol rather than just a shape.
And that's the real question this whole chapter now turns to: once code stops being Rust at all, what is anyone actually promising the other side?
